did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job wishes that his anguish and suffering could be weighed together on scales to show how immense their burden is.
Did you know? Job describes his suffering using the image of arrows from the Almighty whose poison drains his spirit, expressing how deeply he feels wounded by God.

Did you know? Job asks whether a wild donkey brays or an ox bellows without reason. In this way, he argues that even animals do not complain without cause, so his own complaint arises from genuine suffering.
Did you know? The image of tasteless food without salt expresses Job’s feeling that his friends’ words are empty and offer no comfort.
Did you know? Job is not asking for wealth or a practical solution; he is praying that his request will be granted and that God will give him what he hopes for.

Did you know? Although Job asks God to put an end to his suffering, he emphasizes that he has not denied or concealed the words of the Holy One. In other words, he sees value in his honesty even in the midst of his distress.
Did you know? Job asks what strength he has left to keep hoping and prolong his life, presenting ongoing suffering as a test of the limits of human endurance.
Did you know? Job compares his brothers to a treacherous stream—a stream that appears promising but disappoints those who rely on it.

Did you know? The mention of the caravans of Tema and the travelers of Sheba paints a picture of people thirsting for water and waiting for it, only to be disappointed in the end. This illustrates Job’s expectation of comfort from his friends.
Did you know? Despite his sharp rebuke, Job declares that he is willing to listen if his friends can show him where he went wrong and explain his error with truthful words.
